# Lost and Found in Japan

I've wanted to visit Japan for as long as I can remember, and nothing prepared me for how much the country would exceed those expectations.

We landed in Tokyo and were immediately swept into the current of Shibuya Crossing—hundreds of people moving in perfect, chaotic harmony. But my favorite moments were the quiet ones: slurping ramen at a tiny six-seat shop in Shinjuku, watching the city glow through the window.

Ten days felt like both a lifetime and a heartbeat. We flew home, and honestly, I started planning the next trip before we landed.

Sayonara for now, Japan. I'll be back.

**Overview**

Languages never sit still. Words rise and fall. Sounds drift. Grammar bends slowly while slang sprints ahead. Yet experts still debate why some innovations spread widely while others vanish within a single generation. Prior work often examined single snapshots in time. This study instead follows innovation as it happens. The stakes are high: language shapes identity and it molds how groups bond and how knowledge passes between generations. We will examine how language evolves over time by observing new words and new forms as they move through living populations of speakers.

**Aims**

- Map where and when new words and meanings are born in online forums and other digital spaces.
- Measure how fast innovations spread across age bands and world regions.
- Identify which drivers favor retention of novel forms and which ones hasten their loss.
- Test whether Darwinian ideas such as mutation and drift explain observed patterns better than rival models.

**Methods**

We will assemble a large digital library of English text spanning 150 years and drawn from books and newspapers as well as open web forums. Automated tools will flag novel terms and follow each one over time. Machine learning models will estimate spread rates and extrapolate likely future paths. We will also run interviews with speakers from varied age bands to learn why people adopt some innovations and drop others. An oversight board will review every step and all text will be stored with strict safeguards.

**Timeline**

Year one: library assembly and tool design. Year two: data gathering and model building. Year three: interviews and synthesis and paper writing.

**Team**

Our team blends expertise in anthropology and quantitative language studies.

**Results and Value**

We aim to deliver the first unified model of language evolution built from real time-stamped data. Findings will aid editors who maintain word lists and style guides. Findings will also help teams that train large language models and everyone who wants to know where our shared tongue is heading.

**Funding**

We request modest funding for server storage and two graduate assistants and travel for field interviews.

Your friend's advice contains a kernel of truth, but it is not the best method for a bike chain. Coke does contain phosphoric acid, which can chemically react with RUST and help loosen it from metal surfaces. However, the soda also contains a lot of sugar, which leaves a sticky residue on your chain if you do not clean it off THOROUGHLY. That residue will attract dirt and grime, which is the last thing you want on a bicycle drivetrain. The Coke method is also slow and messy compared to alternatives that cost about the same.

The STEEL WOOL part of the advice is where things get more questionable. Steel wool is fairly aggressive and can scratch the metal surfaces of your chain. A bike chain is a precision component with tight tolerances, so you want to avoid anything too abrasive.

A better approach starts with removing the chain from the bike, if possible, so you can soak it. Soak it first in a degreaser to strip away old oil and grime. For the rust itself, white vinegar or a citric acid solution works better than COKE and leaves far less residue. Let the chain soak for twenty to thirty minutes, then scrub it with a stiff NYLON BRUSH or an old toothbrush. A brass brush is another good option because brass is softer than chain steel and will not gouge it.

After scrubbing, rinse the chain with clean water and dry it completely right away. Any leftover moisture will cause fresh rust to form surprisingly fast. Once the chain is bone dry, apply a quality chain LUBRICANT to every link. This step is essential, not optional, because freshly exposed bare metal is extremely vulnerable to corrosion. Wipe off the excess lube so it does not attract dirt while you ride.

Finally, check whether the chain is worn out, since a chain that has been rusty for a long time may be stretched or structurally compromised. So while your friend was not entirely wrong, I would skip the Coke and steel wool combination and go with vinegar, a brush, and proper lubrication instead.

# The Weight of Quiet Things

The winter Jonas turned fourteen, the lake behind their new house froze white from shore to shore. By February the whole town of Holden crossed it daily — kids walking to school, cutting a mile off the road. The ice looked like poured concrete.

Jonas crossed it on a Tuesday with Danny Perrault, and it held. He crossed again on Wednesday. On Thursday, old Einar Voss was waiting at the shoreline with his ice auger and a long face.

"You're walking the middle channel," Einar said.

"So? It's THICK. I can hear it under my boots. Solid as a road."

"Sit down a minute."

Einar drilled a hole near shore. The core came up six inches of pale blue ice, clean and hard. He drilled again twenty feet out, where the snow lay smooth and unbroken, and the core came up milky, full of frozen slush, barely three inches sound.

"Same lake," he said. "Same day. The snow fell early this year and packed down over the middle like a blanket. Blankets don't just keep things WARM, boy. They keep things from freezing. And there's a spring under that channel that never stops moving. Moving water doesn't freeze like standing water. Your eyes tell you one story. The lake is telling you another."

"But it LOOKS solid."

"It does. That's exactly what makes it DANGEROUS. If it looked thin, you'd never go near it. The truths that can hurt you are the ones wearing a good coat."

He made Jonas kneel and press his ear to the ice while he tapped it with the auger handle. Near shore: a bright ring, almost a bell. Over the channel: a flat, dead knock, and beneath it something like a whisper moving.

"Water," Einar said. "Running under three inches of ice that wants to be your road. You can't SEE that. So you have to learn to LISTEN. The loud truths are for tourists. The real ones keep their voices DOWN."

Jonas didn't cross the lake again that winter. In March the paper ran a story about a pickup that went through the ice on a lake twenty miles north. The driver had walked out onto it first and pronounced it safe. It looked safe. It was not.

But the thing Einar taught him did not stay on the ice.

That spring, Jonas's mother started saying she was FINE. She said it in her usual tone, and at first he took it at face value, the way you take a white lake at face value. Then he began to notice what lay underneath the word. Her coffee going cold, half-drunk, three mugs on the counter by noon. The mail sitting unopened for days. His father's coat still hanging by the door, January snow still crusted on the shoulders, and her walking past it EVERY morning without once touching it. She laughed at the right times, same as the ice held weight near the shore. But out in the middle, where it mattered, she was three inches thick over moving water.

He didn't ask if she was okay. That question gets the same answer the lake gives your eyes.

Later, remembering Einar, Jonas understood: the surface of a person will hold you right up until the moment it doesn't. What someone says is the shoreline. What someone means is the channel. They sit under a smooth white skin, quiet and running — waiting for you to drill down and LISTEN, or, if you don't, waiting for the day you walk out onto them with all your weight, certain, because everything looked so solid, right up until it wasn't.

**Department of History — New Course Submission**

**Course Number:** HIST 314 (cross-listed with Animal Studies 314)
**Title:** The History of the World, as Told by Dogs
**Credits:** 3 | **Format:** Two 75-minute lectures plus one discussion section weekly
**Prerequisites:** None. No prior experience with dogs required, though students who smell of other dogs will not be penalized.
**Office Hours:** Held outdoors, weather permitting.

---

## Course Description

This course surveys world history from a vantage point roughly two feet off the ground: the dog's. For at least 15,000 years — long before writing, wheels, or agriculture — dogs have witnessed, enabled, survived, and occasionally derailed the events we call history. Rather than retelling the familiar story of kings and conquests, we follow the hunter, herder, guard, courier, laboratory subject, and lap-warmer who has been present for nearly every chapter of the human story.

We open with the improbable truce between two rival predatory species at the end of the Ice Age and close with the genome-sequenced, orthopedic-bed-owning dogs of the present. Along the way, we ask what history looks like when narrated by an animal with no concept of property (beyond "mine"), no writing system (beyond marking), and an extraordinary memory for smell.

## Learning Objectives

Students who complete this course will be able to:

1. **Explain the domestication story** — evaluate competing theories of how wolves became dogs, including self-domestication and the "survival of the friendliest" hypothesis.
2. **Apply ethological concepts**, such as the canid predatory sequence (orient → eye → stalk → chase → grab-bite), to interpret how selective breeding distributed fragments of wolf behavior across modern breeds: the herder's frozen stalk, the retriever's soft mouth, the terrier's commitment.
3. **Critique anthropocentrism** in historical writing and practice multispecies historiography — "history from below," conducted at ground level.
4. **Interpret non-textual evidence**, including archaeology, art, genomes, and behavior.

## Weekly Schedule (14 Weeks)

1. **Before the Bark:** Wolves, hunters, and the first truce
2. **Reading the Earliest Record:** Fossil jaws, cave art, and the 14,000-year-old Bonn-Oberkassel burial
3. **Divine Dogs:** Anubis, Cerberus, Xolotl, and the dogs of Egypt, Mesopotamia, Mesoamerica, and China
4. **Flocks and Fields:** The Agricultural Revolution, when the predatory chase was repurposed into the herding instinct
5. **War Dogs of the Ancient World:** Assyrian mastiffs to Roman legions
6. **Dogs of Conquest:** Becerrillo and the canine accomplices of empire in the Americas
7. **Lap Dogs and Palaces:** Status, symbolism, and the Pekingese of the Forbidden City
8. **Dogs at the Ends of the Earth:** Ship's dogs, sled dogs, and the age of exploration
9. **The Victorian Invention of the Breed:** Kennel clubs, dog shows, and the selective breeding of status
10. **Dogs in the Laboratory:** Pavlov's employees and the ethics of animal research
11. **Dogs of the World Wars:** Sgt. Stubby, messenger huskies, and Laika's one-way ticket
12. **The Professional Dog:** Guide dogs, detection dogs, and therapy dogs
13. **The Decoded Dog:** What genomics tells us — and what it can't
14. **The Future of the Pack:** Street dogs, conservation dogs, and the question of what we owe them

## Assessment

- **Participation** — 15% (discussion, not fetch)
- **Midterm examination** — 20% (traditional closed-book format; window seats available)
- **Comparative essay** — 25% (2,500 words on the dog's role in two societies)
- **Final project: The Barkchive** — 40% (students produce a primary source from a dog's perspective — a memoir, an "oral history" of a local working dog, a museum exhibit — plus a reflective essay connecting it to course themes)

## Rationale

Animal history is one of the liveliest currents in the discipline, and no animal offers a richer archive than the dog — our co-evolutionary partner, whose story is inseparable from ours at every stage, from the hunt to the genome. Every history is told from somewhere; the dog's somewhere — low to the ground, nose-first, loyal to particular persons rather than abstract nations — will generate genuinely fresh perspectives on familiar material, from agriculture to empire to modern science.

The course also serves as an accessible gateway to methods in multispecies history and animal studies and is expected to draw students broadly across majors. Sample readings include work by Alexandra Horowitz, Brian Hare, and Raymond Coppinger, supplemented by primary sources and one (1) appropriately rigorous set of field observations at the campus quad.

Gideon has several practical options for handling his surplus crops:

## Selling the Surplus

The most common option is to sell the extra crops for profit. He could:
- Sell at a **local farmers' market** or roadside stand
- Negotiate with wholesalers, grocery stores, or restaurants
- Sell directly to consumers through a Community Supported Agriculture (CSA) program
- Explore export opportunities if the surplus is large enough

## Storing for Later

If market prices are low right now, *Gideon could store his surplus in silos, cold storage, or root cellars and wait to sell when prices improve*. He could also preserve crops through canning, freezing, or drying to extend their shelf life.

## Donating to Those in Need

He might donate excess produce to:
- Local food banks and pantries
- Community kitchens or charities
- School lunch programs

## Other Creative Uses

- **Feed livestock** – crops not fit for market often make good animal feed
- **Save seeds** – set aside some harvest for next season's planting
- **Process into value-added products** – turn tomatoes into sauce, fruits into jam, or grains into flour, which can command higher prices
- **Compost or plow under** – return nutrients to the soil for future growing seasons
